module_competencies: Navigate and apply WMO and ICAO regulatory frameworks governing aeronautical meteorology.
Assess airspace classifications and route structures to support aviation planning.
Calculate and apply correct altimetry settings for safe flight operations.
Integrate meteorological factors into fuel consumption and route optimization strategies.

end_of_module_quiz_plan.format: Multiple choice questions testing application, judgment, and interpretation, rather than simple recall. (V2: question pool grown from 15 to 29 across the four lessons during the meteorology-depth expansion.)

lessons.title: International Regulatory Frameworks (WMO & ICAO)
learning_objectives: Outline the roles and responsibilities of the WMO and ICAO in global aviation meteorology.
Interpret key standards and recommended practices (SARPs) relevant to aviation weather forecasting.
Explain the flow of meteorological information between international bodies and local authorities.
Map the core aviation MET products (METAR, TAF, SIGMET, AIRMET) to the Annex 3 chapter and office that govern them.
Distinguish the operational roles of the AMO, MWO, WAFC, VAAC and TCAC in the global service architecture.
Explain the Quality Management System (QMS) and competence requirements an aeronautical MET provider must satisfy.
diagrams_needed: Organizational hierarchy showing the relationship between WMO, ICAO, and National Meteorological Services.
Process flow of how a meteorological standard becomes an operational requirement.

lessons.title: Aviation Route Planning & Fuel Management
learning_objectives: Evaluate the impact of meteorological conditions (e.g., headwinds, temperatures) on route selection.
Calculate the meteorological effects on fuel consumption during various flight phases.
Recommend optimal flight levels based on upper-air forecasts.
Explain why the shortest track is a great circle, and how wind shifts the minimum-time track away from it.
Quantify the effect of ISA temperature deviation on true airspeed, cruise ceiling and fuel flow.
Break dispatch fuel into its components and trace how a forecast error propagates into payload or a diversion.
key_concepts: Fuel Burn Rates and Contingency Fuel
diagrams_needed: System diagram showing inputs for flight planning (weather, aircraft type, route) and resulting fuel calculations.
Annotated cross-section of a flight path showing wind components affecting fuel efficiency.

lessons.title: Airspace Structure & Classification
learning_objectives: Differentiate between various classes of airspace and their operational requirements.
Relate airspace structures to the provision of meteorological services.
Identify controlled, uncontrolled, and special use airspaces.
Describe the nested control hierarchy (FIR/ACC, TMA/Approach, CTR) and the ATS and CVFR route structure.
Apply ICAO visual-meteorological-condition (VMC) minima to decide whether a VFR flight is legal in a given class.
Match each MET product (SIGMET, TAF, TREND, aerodrome and wind-shear warnings, low-level VFR guidance) to the airspace it serves.
diagrams_needed: Visual representation of airspace classes (A to G) showing altitude limits and VFR/IFR rules.
Map schematic illustrating the division of a geographic area into Flight Information Regions (FIRs).

lessons.title: Principles of Aviation Altimetry
learning_objectives: Define and differentiate between QNH, QFE, and Standard Altimeter Settings.
Determine the appropriate transition altitude and transition level for flight operations.
Calculate true altitude based on non-standard temperature and pressure variations.
Explain how the standard atmosphere converts pressure to indicated altitude, and define pressure altitude and density altitude.
Distinguish QNH from the synoptic QFF, and map each setting to its radio phraseology (Altitude, Height, Flight Level).
Apply the Israeli AIP ENR 1.7 transition procedures (QNE above 10,500 ft; regional QNH below FL115).
diagrams_needed: Vertical profile diagram comparing QNH, QFE, and Standard Pressure reference planes.
Decision tree for altimeter setting changes during climb (Transition Altitude) and descent (Transition Level).
